name: Paraguay
summary_text: Paraguay has no legal gender recognition procedure in force. The judiciary has yet to issue final rulings in ten lawsuits filed by trans people seeking recognition of their legal names, among them cases brought by Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepúlveda that have been pending since 2016. Both plaintiffs have taken communications to the UN Human Rights Committee under the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and are awaiting a decision. Trans people are not allowed to change their name and gender on official documents, so a trans visitor whose passport marker conflicts with their presentation has no domestic route to alignment.  Amnesty International's 2025-26 report records two trans migrants who were denied identity documents, evidence that the documentary gap reaches administrative encounters rather than staying theoretical.  There is no general anti-discrimination law covering gender identity or sexual orientation, and no hate-crime statute is recorded in the sources. A November 2015 bill to ban discrimination on those grounds has not advanced since its introduction. Protections that do exist are narrow and sector-specific, addressing sexual orientation in dormitory placement, violence against women, stateless persons, personal data and the internal staffing rules of one public office. None supplies a general remedy to a trans visitor refused service, accommodation or police assistance.  Violence and discrimination against LGBT people remain frequent in Paraguay and are often ignored by the police. An Associated Press report of September 2025 found that discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence push trans women out of their hometowns and into migration and sex work, a pattern that shapes the settings a trans visitor may move through.  Official hostility is documented at national and municipal level alike. The government banned discussion of LGBT issues in public schools in October 2017, and the Minister of Education said he might consider burning books that raise awareness about transgender people. Asunción's city council banned an event honouring a trans human-rights defender who died in March, per Amnesty International. Horacio Cartes, a senior ruling-party figure, said in 2017 that he would "shoot himself in the testicles" if his son married another man, later apologising to those offended.  Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised in Paraguayan law. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights has held in an advisory opinion that OAS signatories must allow same-sex marriage; Paraguay is an OAS party and is bound by the ruling, while domestic law has not been brought into line. A trans visitor's partner therefore has no standing under local law.  Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Paraguay since 1990. The sources record an age of consent of 16 for homosexual conduct and 14 for heterosexual conduct.  Healthcare carries one trans-specific entitlement. Resolution 695, approved by the Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare in October 2016, requires that health service officials record and treat transgender patients under their identified social name on medical records, medical histories and forms. Law 7018 on Mental Health, enacted 15 November 2022, states that a mental health diagnosis cannot be made on the exclusive basis of sexual choice or identity.

sources.title: Inter-American Court of Human Rights (IACHR) Advisory Opinion OC-24/17
sources.documents: Requires states party to American Convention on Human Rights, including Paraguay, to grant same-sex couples access to marriage and all rights deriving from marriage.
sources.detail: Cited as issued 8 January 2018 / 9 January 2018 advisory opinion; basis for SOMOSGAY petition to Supreme Court of Justice announced 12 January 2018
